promptText: What is an "agent registry," and why does an enterprise need one instead of letting teams deploy agents freely?
options: A logging tool that only records failed tool calls

A central, authoritative catalog of every agent — who owns it, what it can access, what model it's pinned to, and which version is live — without which the organization cannot answer basic questions like how many agents exist or what they can touch during a security review
A caching layer that speeds up repeated tool calls
A billing dashboard exclusively for tracking token spend
explanation: Without a registry, teams deploy agents independently and the organization ends up with 'agent sprawl,' making both security review and compliance audits practically impossible.

promptText: Why should an agent have its own dedicated identity/credentials instead of sharing the calling application's existing service account?
options: Dedicated identities are required by the MCP specification
Sharing credentials collapses attribution and makes it impossible to scope the agent's permissions more narrowly than whatever the shared credential already allows
Shared credentials are always more expensive to operate
Dedicated identities make the agent run measurably faster
explanation: A dedicated identity per agent lets you grant least-privilege access and unambiguously attribute every action back to a specific agent and version.

promptText: What two axes does "risk tiering" classify agent actions along to decide whether human approval is required?
options: Token cost and response latency
Reversibility (can a mistake be undone?) and blast radius (how much/how many does a mistake affect?)
Model size and prompt length
Number of tools available and number of agents involved
explanation: Low-risk, reversible, narrow-impact actions can run autonomously; irreversible or large-blast-radius actions are gated behind mandatory human approval regardless of the agent's confidence.

promptText: What role does an "agent gateway" play in an enterprise agent platform?
options: It is a UI dashboard for viewing agent conversation transcripts

It is the single enforcement point every tool call must pass through, checking scope, data classification, budget, and risk tier before letting a call through, denying it, or routing it to human approval — architecturally the same pattern as an API gateway
It is a load balancer that only distributes traffic across model providers
It replaces the need for an agent registry entirely
explanation: Rather than trusting every agent's LLM-driven decision to behave correctly, the gateway inserts a mediating policy layer, so the agent never has direct, unmediated access to sensitive systems.

promptText: According to the chapter's historical framing, what pattern does LLM-driven "agent sprawl" most directly repeat from a prior technology wave?
options: The mainframe-to-client-server migration of the 1980s

RPA "bot sprawl" from 2015-2020 — orphaned bots under departed employees' credentials, no central inventory, and silent breakage — for which the fix was a bot registry, service-account identities, and change control
The introduction of relational databases in the 1970s
The shift from on-premises to cloud hosting
explanation: The chapter frames this as the third repetition of a pattern enterprise architecture already solved twice (API sprawl in the SOA era, then bot sprawl in the RPA era), just now with non-deterministic LLM-driven actors.

promptText: Why is enforcing idempotency on every side-effecting agent tool call important?
options: It reduces the number of tokens consumed per model call
It ensures a retried or duplicated invocation (from a crash, a timeout, or the agent's own confused re-attempt) cannot double-execute an action, such as issuing a refund twice
It is required only for tools that read data, never for tools that write data
It allows the agent to skip the human approval step entirely
explanation: Because an LLM-driven plan can non-deterministically re-attempt a step after a partial failure with no fixed, auditable retry logic, idempotency keys are the safeguard against duplicate side effects.

promptText: Using Little's Law (L = λ × W), why does a policy of "require human approval for every risky agent action" fail to scale as agent adoption grows?
options: Little's Law shows that queue length decreases automatically as more agents are added

As more agents propose approval-requiring actions, the arrival rate λ grows, but reviewer headcount and review time W don't shrink automatically, so the approval queue length (and every agent's wait time) grows roughly linearly — the sustainable fix is reducing λ via tighter risk tiering, not adding reviewers indefinitely
Little's Law only applies to network queueing, not to human approval workflows
The law proves that approval queues never actually reach a steady state
explanation: Since reviewer headcount cannot scale as fast as software, risk tiering is the only lever that keeps the arrival rate of approval-requiring actions bounded as agent adoption scales.

promptText: Why is idempotency more important for an LLM-driven agent's tool calls than for a traditional, fixed-script RPA bot's actions?
options: RPA bots never make mistakes, so idempotency was never a concern for them

An LLM-driven plan can non-deterministically re-attempt or rephrase a step after a partial failure with no fixed, human-authored retry block to inspect in advance, since the 'script' is regenerated at run time rather than fixed
Idempotency is actually less important for agents because agents always run in a single-threaded loop
RPA bots use a completely different network protocol that makes retries automatically safe
explanation: A fixed RPA script's retry logic is auditable and predetermined; an agent's retry behavior emerges dynamically from model reasoning, so idempotency keys are the deterministic safeguard against duplicate side effects.

promptText: Why is a global "kill switch" or instant rollback capability considered essential, yet often missing in early agent implementations?
options: Because model providers require it as a contractual condition of API access

Because agent behavior driven by non-deterministic model output can start misbehaving subtly (confidently wrong actions, not a crash) after a model update or prompt change, and without a registry-level ability to disable or revert instantly, the only remediation under incident pressure is a slow, risky full redeploy
Because it is the only way to measure per-tenant cost
Because without it, agents cannot call any external tools at all
explanation: Early implementations miss this because they treat the agent as just another feature flag off a codebase rather than a versioned, governed artifact needing an instant, registry-level rollback path.

promptText: How does SOX compliance shape what an agent may do autonomously in a finance workflow?
options: SOX bans any use of AI agents in financial workflows entirely

SOX requires segregation of duties: an agent cannot both initiate and approve a financially material transaction, so a human or independently-controlled system must approve any agent-proposed action that could affect financial statements, with an immutable, reviewable record of what evidence was used
SOX only applies to publicly disclosed model architectures, not to agent behavior
SOX requires that agents always use the most capable available model for financial tasks
explanation: The same segregation-of-duties principle that applies to human employees applies to the agent, and SOX audits look for exactly that control evidence.

promptText: What does the "agent-as-employee" mental model suggest as the equivalent of a new employee's probation period for a newly-deployed agent?
options: Deploying the agent directly to full production traffic on day one to gather maximum data quickly
A staged rollout — shadow mode, then approval-required, then autonomous — gated by observed accuracy, mirroring how a new employee earns increasing autonomy over time
Requiring the agent to pass a one-time certification exam before any deployment, with no further evaluation afterward
Giving the agent broad, unscoped access immediately so it can prove its full capability range
explanation: Every governance mechanism in the chapter maps onto a human-employee equivalent; the probation period maps to a staged rollout gated by observed, evidence-backed accuracy rather than a one-time launch check.

promptText: What are the two components of agent cost, according to the chapter's cost-accounting formula, and why does this make cost easy to underestimate?
options: Only the model's per-token price matters; downstream tool costs are negligible

Cost(run) sums tokens consumed per step across every reasoning step plus downstream system cost per tool call — a plan that loops five extra times due to an ambiguous tool result costs five times as much, invisibly, unless every step is metered individually rather than only at the end
Cost is a fixed, flat fee per agent regardless of how many steps it takes
Cost only depends on the number of distinct agents deployed, not on individual run behavior
explanation: Because cost is a sum over every step and every tool call, near-real-time per-step metering is necessary to catch a runaway loop mid-execution rather than discovering it on next month's invoice.

promptText: A VP asks why every new agent must go through a shared registry, gateway, and eval-gated pipeline instead of letting product teams "just ship it." What is the strongest justification, per the chapter's framing?
options: Shared infrastructure is required purely because it is the current industry trend

The organization has already paid this exact tuition twice — API sprawl in the SOA era and bot sprawl in the RPA era — both eventually fixed by the same shared infrastructure pattern; the cost of the shared platform is paid once, while the cost of not having it is paid repeatedly and unpredictably, usually during an incident
Shared infrastructure guarantees the agent's reasoning will always be correct
Product teams are legally prohibited from building their own AI integrations
explanation: Without a shared registry nobody can answer 'what agents exist and what can they touch' during a security review; without a shared gateway every team implements authorization inconsistently; without an eval-gated pipeline there's no fast rollback path.

promptText: Two VPs disagree: one wants centralized governance to slow rollout for safety, the other wants decentralized ownership to move fast. What resolution does the chapter's reasoning suggest?
options: Pick whichever VP has more organizational seniority and apply their preferred model uniformly across all agents

Reframe away from a single global choice: scale the degree of centralization with the risk tier of the action — low-risk, easily-reversible actions get a fast, largely decentralized path, while high-risk, hard-to-reverse actions go through fuller centralized review regardless of which business unit owns the agent
Apply full centralization to every agent to eliminate any possibility of disagreement in the future
Apply full decentralization to every agent so no team is ever blocked by another team's review
explanation: This risk-proportionate design gives the velocity-focused VP genuine speed on most low-risk use cases and gives the safety-focused VP genuine rigor on the smaller set of cases that actually warrant it, rather than an all-or-nothing political compromise.

promptText: What is "agent TCO" (total cost of ownership), and what two components does the chapter say are most commonly underestimated when projecting an agent's ROI?
options: TCO is just the model API bill; nothing else is commonly underestimated

TCO sums build cost, ongoing compute/tool cost, human review labor, incident remediation, and continuous evaluation overhead over the agent's lifetime — human review time (teams assume the agent fully replaces a human, then discover ongoing review is still needed) and continuous evaluation cost (the one-time pilot eval gets mistakenly treated as done) are the most commonly underestimated components
TCO only includes the platform team's engineering salaries
TCO is calculated once at launch and never needs to be revisited
explanation: Both underestimated components tend to erode a rosy initial ROI projection well after the launch decision has already been celebrated, since production drift requires ongoing evaluation investment for as long as the agent runs.
